title: The Lord Brings His Case Against Judah
summary: The Lord calls heaven and earth to witness as he accuses his people of rebellion: they are like children who turned against a father and a land beaten until nothing is sound. He rejects their sacrifices and festivals because their hands are full of blood, calls them to wash, seek justice, and defend the fatherless and the widow, and offers to make scarlet sins white as snow. Jerusalem, once faithful, has become corrupt, and God promises to purge her and make her again the Faithful City.
story: Isaiah opens not with the prophet's call (that comes in chapter 6) but with a summons to court. By the eighth century BC the people of Judah had been in the land for centuries, had a temple in Jerusalem and a king from David's line, and kept an elaborate round of sacrifices and feasts. The covenant God made with Israel at Sinai promised blessing for faithfulness and warned of devastation for rebellion (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). This chapter declares that the warnings have begun to come true. Many scholars see it as an overture to the whole book, gathering themes that will return: rebellion, a remnant, corrupt worship, justice for the weak, purifying judgment, and a restored Zion. Its final images of burning and of gardens are taken up again in the book's last chapter.
historical:
The heading (verse 1) places Isaiah's work in the reigns of four kings of Judah: Uzziah (also called Azariah), Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Together these span roughly the second half of the eighth century BC and the start of the seventh. Uzziah's long reign had been prosperous (2 Chronicles 26), but the prosperity bred complacency and injustice, the same problems Isaiah's contemporaries Amos and Micah denounced. Meanwhile Assyria, under Tiglath-pileser III and his successors, was expanding west toward Judah.

Verses 7 and 8 describe a land burned and occupied by foreigners, with Jerusalem left alone like a shack in a field. Many scholars connect this with the Assyrian king Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC, when he captured the fortified cities of Judah and besieged Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:13), and Sennacherib's own annals boast of taking forty-six of Hezekiah's walled towns. If so, this chapter, though placed first, may come from late in Isaiah's ministry and was set at the front because it summarizes his message. Others connect it with the earlier attack by Aram and Israel around 735 BC. The chapter itself does not say.
cultural:
Isaiah uses the form of a lawsuit. Ancient treaties between kings and vassals often called gods and cosmic powers as witnesses, and Israel's covenant had heaven and earth as its witnesses (Deuteronomy 30:19; 32:1). By opening with “Listen, O heavens, and give ear, O earth”, Isaiah signals that the covenant's terms are being enforced. The images are from daily life: an ox and a donkey know where they are fed, a watchman's shelter in a vineyard stands alone after the harvest, and silver is refined by melting away the dross.

The worship Isaiah describes was the lawful worship of the temple: burnt offerings, New Moons (the monthly festival at the new moon), Sabbaths, and appointed feasts. The problem was not the rituals themselves, which God had commanded, but that they were offered by people whose hands were covered with blood and who ignored the fatherless and the widow. In Israel's law, orphans and widows were the classic examples of people without a male protector or legal advocate, and God repeatedly names himself as their defender (Deuteronomy 10:18). The sacred oaks and gardens of verse 29 were places of fertility worship borrowed from Canaanite religion.
literary: The chapter is a collection of shorter oracles woven into a single argument. It moves from accusation (verses 2-9) to the rejection of worship without justice (verses 10-17), to an offer and a choice (verses 18-20), to a lament over Jerusalem and a promise of purifying judgment (verses 21-31). Parallelism runs through it, as in all Hebrew poetry: a line is echoed or extended in the next. Verses 9 and 10 pivot on Sodom and Gomorrah: only a remnant has kept Judah from becoming like them, and yet its rulers act like the rulers of Sodom. Verses 21 to 26 form a ring: the city that was faithful and full of justice will again be called the Faithful City. The chapter ends with fire, a picture of judgment that consumes the strong and their works together.

outline.t: The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz
A rebellious people and a beaten land
Worship God refuses and the justice he requires
The faithful city corrupted and restored
Redemption for the penitent, fire for the rebels

doctrines.note: Sin here is rebellion against a Father who raised his children, a failure to know God that is worse than an ox's ignorance. It shows itself especially in injustice and bloodshed, and it corrupts even worship.

The call of verses 16 and 17 shows what repentance means: to stop doing evil, learn to do good, and seek justice for the weak. Verse 18 offers full cleansing, and verses 19 and 20 set the choice between obedience and rebellion.
God's judgment in this chapter is a refining fire. He will purge the dross from Jerusalem so that she can again be the City of Righteousness, while those who refuse to turn will be consumed.
The title the Holy One of Israel appears in verse 4, the first of many uses in Isaiah. God's holiness is why empty worship offends him and why he insists on justice.

words.note: Qadosh, holy. In verse 4 it appears in Isaiah's signature title for God, the Holy One of Israel. The word marks what is set apart and wholly other, and in Isaiah it describes God's moral purity and majesty. That the Holy One is of Israel means he has bound himself to this people, which makes their rebellion so grave.

Yakach, to argue, decide, or rebuke, translated reason together in verse 18. It is a legal word: to settle a case in court. God is not inviting a casual discussion but calling the accused to face the verdict, and then surprising them with an offer of cleansing.

Mishpat, justice. It means the right ordering of relationships in a community, especially through fair judgment for those who cannot defend themselves. Isaiah uses it three times here; Jerusalem was once full of it (verse 21) and will be redeemed by it (verse 27).

Pasha, to rebel or transgress. The word was used for a vassal breaking faith with his overlord, and it is the first charge God brings: I raised children, and they rebelled against me (verse 2). Sin is personal betrayal, not only the breaking of a rule.

christ: This chapter prepares for the gospel mainly by showing the problem it answers. Paul quotes verse 9 in Romans 9:29 to argue that God has always preserved a remnant by grace. The offer of verse 18, sins like scarlet made white as snow, is fulfilled in the New Testament's proclamation that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7) and that his people are washed (Revelation 7:14). Jesus stood in the same prophetic line when he cleansed the temple and when he rebuked those who kept the details of worship while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23). The promise that Zion will be redeemed by justice and righteousness points ahead to the king of Isaiah 9 and 11, who will rule with both, and whom Christians identify with Jesus.

hard.q: Did God reject the sacrifices he himself commanded?
hard.a: Verses 11 to 15 sound as though God hates the whole system of worship he gave in Leviticus. Some older critical scholars took passages like this, along with Amos 5:21-24 and Hosea 6:6, as evidence that the prophets opposed ritual altogether. Most interpreters today read it differently. The prophets were not against worship but against worship cut off from obedience. The key line is verse 15: God will not listen because their hands are covered with blood. The Hebrew Bible often uses this kind of absolute contrast to express priority (compare 1 Samuel 15:22, where obedience is better than sacrifice). Worship that treats God as a patron to be paid while the poor are crushed is not worship of the God of Israel at all. The same prophet who condemns these offerings will later describe God's house as a house of prayer for all nations (56:7).

questions: God says he will not listen to prayers from people whose hands are full of blood. How does the way we treat vulnerable people affect our worship?
Verse 18 offers cleansing to people who deserve judgment. How does that offer change the way you think about your own failures?
Jerusalem was once faithful and became corrupt. How does gradual compromise happen in a person or a church, and what guards against it?
